title: Will the United States attack Oman before 2027?
resolution_criteria: This question will resolve as **Yes** if, before January 1, 2027, the United States carries out a military attack against Oman's territory or military forces. This can be purposefully or accidentally.
fine_print:
Oman's territory includes territorial waters.

To qualify, the attack will need to target or physically harm Omani buildings, infrastructure, vessels, military forces, or nationals. Cyberattacks, warning shots, and strikes that cause no such harm will not count, regardless of where they land.

If it is disputed whether the United States is responsible for an attack, this question will refer to credible sources or may resolve as **ambiguous**. In case of an attack where there is no credible source consensus that it occurred within Oman's territory and neither the US nor Oman claims that it did, this question will not resolve based on that incident.

comments.author: sheikah

comments.text:
@(Deranged_saint)

I partially agreed on the frame, but 13% is too high. Threat-to-execution is 0 for 2 with a test in between. Trump threatened Oman on 27 May and 17 August. Nine days after the second, Oman and Iran announced the phased strait framework, exactly the "getting in the way" the threat named. Nothing followed. The rationale was removed on 25 August when the US Navy cleared the Hormuz mines itself. The Oman track is de-escalating even as the Iran track escalates. The embassy returned to routine visa services on 1 September. Markets agree. Oman 5Y CDS is about 77bp versus Saudi at 54bp, below its own March war-start reading of about 89bp. The 17 August threat moved it about 4bp.

On (5) the chain runs backward. Striking Oman adds an oil risk premium rather than crashing prices. A crash needs Hormuz reopened, which an attack through the mediation channel would destroy. Anyway, this is a big game theory model pivoted on Trump in the center, who is a very unpredictable figure, so the 13% may seem high but may be a hedge on that as wel

comments.author: Deranged_saint

comments.text:
(YES\=\<1%)
1\. Temporal Political Constraints
The forecast resolves before 2027, leaving a roughly 113-day window that directly overlaps with the climax of the 2026 US midterm elections and the subsequent lame-duck legislative session. The domestic political capital required to initiate an unprovoked conflict with a stabilizing regional partner during this window is non-existent.
2\. Bilateral Defense & Logistics Architecture
Facilities Access Agreement (1980, amended 2019): The United States maintains explicit operational access to Omani airbases (Masirah Island, Thumrait, RAFO Musannah) and deep-water ports.
Port of Duqm Strategic Value: Located outside the Strait of Hormuz on the Arabian Sea, Duqm allows US Navy carrier strike groups and nuclear-powered submarines to dock, refuel, and conduct heavy maintenance without risking entry into Persian Gulf littoral chokepoints. Attacking Oman would instantaneously dismantle this logistics posture.
3\. Muscat as the Indispensable Diplomatic Conduit
Oman functions as the primary neutral interlocutor between the United States and regional adversaries. This includes indispensable backchannel diplomacy with the Islamic Republic of Iran, de-escalation mediation with the Houthi movement in Yemen throughout 2023–2026, and facilitating complex prisoner exchanges.
The US foreign policy and defense establishments rely heavily on Omani neutrality to manage crisis escalation in the Middle East.
4\. Complete Absence of Casus Belli
Zero Territorial/Ideological Friction: Oman poses zero offensive threat to US territory, assets, or allies.
Institutional Alignment: Oman is a founding member of the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC), participates in combined maritime task forces (CMF/CTF-150/151), and operates US-origin defense hardware.
Conclusion: The probability that the United States initiates an offensive military attack against Oman in the remaining 113 days of 2026 is \<1%, resolving decisively in the negative.

comments.text: @(darkives) Yeah, I agree, but I think including this would mean that users would have to forecast on the probability that Oman strenuously objects, which is pretty random and is best avoided I think. Thanks for your input.

comments.author: darkives
comments.text:
@(skmmcj) The main distance I see between @(tejvn)'s suggestion and the fine print currently is if the U.S. attacks a third party's vessel within Omani territorial waters, *and Oman strenuously objects to this as a violation of their sovereignty*, the question would not resolve as Yes under the current criteria but would resolve as Yes per tejvn.

Maybe we think that this is very unlikely to happen and thus not a big deal. But if it did happen, I would think that tejvn's criteria would match the intuitive result. That said, I don't feel strongly about it—just my two cents.
